title: Highland Whisky Explained | Craft Beer School
desc: What Highland whisky means on a Scotch label, why the region covers such a range of styles and how to taste across it.
teaser: The Highlands are Scotland's biggest whisky region. That is why no single flavour can sum them up.
standfirst: Highland whisky covers more ground than any other Scotch region, from the far north coast to the edge of Glasgow and out to many of the islands. Expect variety rather than a single house style. Here is how the region is defined, how its styles differ and how to taste your way around it.
sections: The biggest region on the map

Scotland has five protected whisky regions and localities under the Scotch Whisky Regulations 2009: Highland, Lowland, Speyside, Campbeltown and Islay. The Highland region is by far the largest. It covers most of the country north of a line drawn roughly from Greenock on the River Clyde to Dundee on the River Tay.

Speyside sits inside the Highland region as its own protected locality. The islands other than Islay, such as Skye, Mull, Jura and Orkney, fall within the Highland region legally, though many writers group them informally as the Islands. Our guide to Speyside whisky covers the busiest corner of the region.
Why there is no single Highland style

A region this large holds coastal and inland distilleries, mountain glens and farmland, old sites and new ones. Each distillery's stills, fermentation, cut points and casks do more to shape its whisky than the region does. So Highland on a label tells you where the whisky was made, not what it tastes like.

Writers often split the Highlands informally by compass point. These groupings are useful shorthand, not legal categories. Every one has exceptions.

• Northern Highlands: coastal distilleries often produce rich, waxy or maritime malts, sometimes with a hint of salt and spice.
  • Eastern Highlands: often fruity, malty and full bodied, with some distilleries using sherry casks for depth.
  • Southern Highlands: lighter, softer and gentler, closer in feel to some Lowland whiskies.
  • Western Highlands: fewer distilleries, sometimes with light peat and a coastal character.

Taste across these groups and the idea of one Highland flavour falls apart quickly.

The island distilleries add more range again. Orkney malts often combine heather, honey and a light smoke. Skye is known for peppery, smoky malt. Jura and Mull have their own styles, some peated and some not. Because they are legally Highland, these whiskies can use Highland on the label, though most simply name their island.

For a taster, island whiskies are a good bridge between the gentle mainland malts and the heavy smoke of Islay.

Most mainland Highland malts are unpeated or lightly peated. A few distilleries make more heavily peated spirit and many used more peat in the past when it was the local kiln fuel. Highland peat formed inland from heather and woody plants is often described as giving a drier, earthier smoke than coastal Islay peat.

Our guide to how whisky is made explains where peat enters the process.

Highland single malts are widely available in India alongside Speyside and Islay. Because the region is so varied, it is a good place to train your palate: you can find a light, floral malt and a rich, sherried one under the same regional name. A Highland malt with a splash of water suits a relaxed evening meal. Rich, sherry cask Highland malts can stand up to slow cooked dishes such as a Lucknowi korma.

Pour small, drink water alongside and never drive after drinking.

The Highland line in whisky goes back to excise law in the late eighteenth century. Distillers north of the line were taxed and regulated differently from those in the Lowlands. Different rules encouraged different practices: Lowland distillers tended to work at larger scale for the English market, while Highland distillers worked smaller.

Those old tax rules are long gone, but the boundary survived into modern labelling. That is why a whisky distilled just north of the line can call itself Highland while one a short drive south is Lowland, even if the two taste more alike than either does to a malt from the far north coast.

Regions record history as much as flavour. Read them that way.
How to taste across the region

Pick two Highland malts from different corners, such as a northern coastal malt and a southern one. Pour 20 ml of each. Nose them side by side and note the differences in fruit, texture and any smoke. Taste neat, then with a few drops of water. You will find far more difference between those two than the shared regional name suggests.

Your first step: look up where on the map your favourite Highland whisky is made, then try one from the opposite side of the region.
faqs: What area does Highland whisky cover?
Most of Scotland north of a line roughly from Greenock to Dundee, including the islands other than Islay. Speyside sits inside it as a separate protected locality.
Legally, yes. The islands other than Islay fall within the Highland region, though many writers group them informally as the Islands.
What does Highland whisky taste like?
There is no single style. Northern coastal malts can be waxy and maritime, eastern ones fruity and malty, southern ones lighter and western ones lightly peated.
